chapter_theme: Songs at Thirukkazhukundram (திருக்கழுக்குன்றம்), the Vedagiri worshipped by eagles: the poet confesses a life spent on women, children and gold until grey age and Yama's rope, and the sea of birth sunk in passion; the praise centres on Murugan as Sambandar and as the teacher of the pranava who bowed at the hunter girl's feet.
structure_note: 541 and 543 follow the two halves; 542 is praise only, a portrait of Murugan as Sambandar; 544 is a short song whose plea is only for the wisdom to love him. 543 is built throughout on doubled sound-words (தனா தனா, பளீர் பளீர், குகா குகா).

541.reading: The poet tells how, struck by Kama's arrows that waste a life, he sank in the sea of lies of laughing kohl-eyed women and fell into sorrow, then took this world as real, clung to children and gold, and grew weak, breathless, bilious and grey; he asks that before he is caught in Yama's rope Murugan grant him grace to be like the good devotees whose minds never leave devotion to his flower feet. The praise names Siva who burned Kama and the three cities with a laugh and a smoking eye, Vishnu the discus-bearer who set enmity among men so that sons and grandsons perished in war, and Murugan who hid his kadamba-garlanded shoulders in a strange disguise to embrace the girl of the millet field, at Thirukkazhukundram, equal to the city of the gods.
541.nuance: The life moves in stages: Kama's arrows and the women, then இகத்தை மெய்க்கொண்டு, taking this world as true, with children (பாலர்) and gold, then old age, then எமக்கயிறு, Yama's rope. The goal is not release but equality with the devotees (நற்றொண்டர்க்கு இணையாக). The discus-bearer who set kin against kin so that all their sons died (புத்திரர் சேயர் அசனைத்தும் செற்றிட) points to Krishna and the Bharata war; the text does not name it.

542.reading: A song of praise only: Murugan is the one whose mouth is fragrant with the nectar that welled from the breast of the first Goddess, whom Vishnu, Brahma and Rudra call their Lady; the pure one of wisdom among the Kauniyas of Kazhi, the hero-poet and guru who made the palm leaf of Tamil swim against the stream and sent the Jains to the stake; the son of Siva who plays with axe, deer, skull, drum, trident and bell; the one who imprisoned Brahma; and the lord of the banana grove at Vedagiri, where eagles worship and the Vedas and Tamil are recited like the sea's roar.
542.nuance: Every detail of the second quatrain is Sambandar's: the Goddess's milk, the Kauniya clan of Kazhi (Sirkazhi), the leaf floated upstream and the impaled Jains. Here they are Murugan's own deeds. கழுகுதொழு வேதகிரி names the eagles of Thirukkazhukundram, and மறைதமிழ்கள் ஓது sets the Vedas and Tamil side by side. One glyph is corrupt (முலையினு஡றி for முலையினூறி).

543.reading: The poet describes lovemaking in a run of doubled sound-words, bees humming, hands clapping on the head, anklets tinkling, birds crying in the throat, sweat running, hair bristling, and asks whether, sunk in the sea of birth and unable to rise, his heart will ever come to think of the six syllables and cry 'Guha, Guha'. The praise, in the same doubled words, shows Sura's garlanded heads red, his teeth white and arms black, his chest crushed, ghouls leaping, the sea dried up and the people crying out, as Murugan took up the vel; it ends at the Tamil Veda hill, Vedagiri, with the son of Siva who married the hunter girl.
543.nuance: The sound-doubling (சலா சலா, சிலீர் சிலீர்) runs through both halves, so that the cure, குகா குகா, comes in the same form as the passion. ஆறெழுத்து, the six syllables, is Murugan's mantra. பவசாகரம், the sea of birth, is where the scene ends. Two corrupt words (வி஡ணர் வி஡ணரென, probably விரீர் விரீரென) and a gap in நிணங்கள்ழு ழுவென leave the doubled words of two lines uncertain.

544.reading: A short song: the poet asks the twelve-shouldered god, who at the right moment bowed his vetchi-crowned head to the lotus feet of the lovely hunter girl in the millet field on Vedagiri, to tell him the wisdom by which he may love him with love. The praise names him as the one who, to the shame of the sage, taught the six syllables within the one syllable to the lord who had taught the gods, so that he too learned.
544.nuance: ஓரெழுத்தில் ஆறெழுத்தை ஓதுவித்த, teaching the six syllables within the one, joins Om to Murugan's six-syllable mantra. The taught one (இமையோரை ஓதுவித்த நாதர்) is Siva, and the shamed sage (முநி நாண) is probably Brahma. The line காதுமுக்ர வீரபத்ர காளி வெட்க is unclear to me.

links.note: Both picture a man who clings to house and desire into a failing old age. The Naladiyar's old man, toothless on his staff, still has his eyes on desire and so has no path to safety; 541's clings to children and gold until he is grey and breathless, and asks for grace before Yama's rope catches him.

source_issues: Song 542: முலையினு஡றி has the corrupt glyph ஡ for ஊ (முலையினூறி).
Song 543: வி஡ணர் வி஡ணரென is corrupt (probably விரீர் விரீரென, with ஡ண for ரீ); the line நிணங்கள்ழு ழுவென has lost a syllable.
